items.s: The café ____ in 2019.
Customers ____ plastic bags to the café.

tfn.s: The café opened with help from the local authorities.
tfn.why: The text says it opened in 2019 "with support from the local authorities".

tfn.s: Customers need to bring two kilograms of plastic for a meal.
tfn.why: The text says one kilogram of plastic gets a full meal.

tfn.s: Customers can choose their meal from a long menu.
tfn.why: The text lists some food but does not say customers can choose.

tfn.s: The writer says one small café cannot solve India's plastic problem.
tfn.why: The text says "one small café cannot solve India's plastic problem on its own".

tfn.s: Waste collectors usually earn a lot of money from selling plastic.
tfn.why: The text says the money they get is "often very small".

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the two words together.

tfn.s: A collector who hands over plastic at the café is rewarded on the same day.
tfn.why: The text says the exchange happens "on the same day rather than at the end of a long month".

tfn.s: The café is the city's main way of dealing with waste.
tfn.why: The text says the café "was never intended to be the city's entire environmental strategy".

tfn.s: Most of the café's customers are informal collectors.
tfn.why: The text does not say who the customers are.

tfn.s: Some people might say the café makes poverty easier to live with without fixing it.
tfn.why: Critics are said to wonder if it "merely makes them slightly easier to live with".

tfn.s: Plastic that nobody collects disappears within a few years.

focus.note: Some phrasal verbs have two small words, like put up with. Learn the whole chunk, not just the first part.

tfn.s: A meal at the café has a more predictable value to a collector than the money from selling scrap.
tfn.why: The text contrasts "a fluctuating scrap price" with a meal, "a known quantity".

tfn.s: The writer sees the amount of plastic removed as the café's main achievement.
tfn.why: The writer calls the tonnage "a drop in the ocean" and looks for its real achievement elsewhere.

tfn.s: Other Indian cities have copied the café's approach.
tfn.why: The text never mentions other cities or imitations.

tfn.s: The writer thinks schemes like this work best alongside regular waste collection.
tfn.why: They "work best when they sit on top of functioning collection services, not in place of them".

tfn.s: The text claims a compassionate policy will necessarily tackle the causes of poverty.
tfn.why: It says a policy "can be compassionate and still leave the structural causes of poverty entirely untouched".

focus.note: Many C1 phrasal verbs are formal or figurative. Notice the idea behind the particle: out means gradually removing, down means taking firm action.

speak.title: Role-play: one kilogram, or nothing?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.text: The rule is one kilogram of plastic for one meal. A collector arrives with a bit less. Ask what is in the bag and why it is light. You can say no, or find a fair solution.

b.text: You've worked all day and your bag is a little under one kilogram. You haven't eaten. Explain your day and ask for a meal. Offer something in return.

phrases: I've been collecting since early this morning.
It's only a bit under a kilogram.
I'm sorry, but the rule is the same for everyone.
Could you make an exception just this once?
I'd be happy to give you a smaller meal.
That's fair, I'll bring more tomorrow.
speak.after: Afterwards, tell the class: was the manager's decision fair, and would you have decided the same?
